Feral

/FEER-ul/ · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Feral means wild and untamed, especially of a domesticated species now living without human contact.

Feral means wild and untamed, especially of a domesticated species now living without human contact. Three generations after the ranch closed, its horses had gone completely feral and would not let a rider within fifty metres.

Worked Example

When the last cannery on the harbour shut in 1994, the cats that had lived on its scraps stayed on. Thirty years and many generations later, the colony under the pier hunts rats at night, dens in the ruined boiler house, and scatters the instant a person steps onto the boards. The volunteers who leave food there have never touched an adult. These animals belong to the same species as the tabby asleep on a nearby windowsill, yet they are now entirely feral.

The colony is a domestic species that has lived generations without human contact and bolts from any person, and that return to wildness is what feral means.

How Feral Sits Among Its Neighbors

Synonyms — open each to see how it differs

untamed

untamed: not domesticated or under human control

wild

wild: living free of human keeping

Antonyms

domesticated

domesticated: bred and kept by humans over generations

tame

tame: accustomed to people and safe to handle

How Strong Is It? — stray → savage → feral

stray vs. feral

stray vs. feral: A stray is a domestic animal that has wandered off but still seeks people out, while feral goes further and describes animals that have stopped depending on us at all.

savage vs. feral

savage vs. feral: Savage is stronger and more judgemental than feral, since it implies ferocity, while a feral goat or cat may simply be shy and self-sufficient.

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — fer-

Root — fer-: wild (Latin ferus)

Suffix — -al

Suffix — -al: relating to; of the kind of

Put it together

Put it together: Latin ferus meant 'wild,' and fera meant a wild animal, the word behind the beasts in a Roman arena. English borrowed the adjective as feral and reserved it, in careful use, for tame stock gone back to the wild. The same root growls through ferocious and through the older word fierce.

Use the root in a new word: ferocious

Use the root in a new word: ferocious: A ferocious storm is 'wild' in the oldest sense of the word, from the same Latin ferus that stands behind feral.
